title: Token Efficiency
author: Maximus200820
selftext:
How do you guys handle token efficiency during development? I’m chugging through my daily limits in 20 minutes. I’m sure it’s a combination of my workflow and only having a $20 subscription, but I’m amazed when I see people that “built a world in a week.”

Im working on a farming roguelite and my current workflow is GPT desktop app > integration agent > review agent > GPT desktop app. Rise & repeat. I’m using the agents in VS code/codex, but it’s taken me 3 days to implement a very basic action/farming system and some debugging/testing tools. I hit my limit very fast and I’m not even at the point of adding visuals yet.

Do I really just need to upgrade to a $100 subscription or is my workflow the issue? Or both?

replies.author: HuWeiliu
replies.body:
Don't feel like you need to ask humans for these answers. Spin up processes to test the quality of different models against the different tasks you do and then once you have data automatically route certain tasks to certain models.
Other people's results might not match up to your own as everyone's projects are different.

comments.author: Rich-Championship944
comments.body:
One big thing that’s helped me better manage usage is creating internal tools for processes such as asset creation and refinement, unit testing, and optimization. 

Before I would just ask Claude to handle it but then it would need to read the context and build the script. Now it references my pre-built tools and uses those.

I’ve also tried to make the back and forth iterations recursive regarding efficiency. Simply aiming to make the agents leaner atm.

comments.author: Jessica___
comments.body:
Here's what I do: 

Sol/opus for planning, Luna/Haiku for implementation, sol/opus for reviewing the implementation.

Always create new chats, each new task or sub task = new chat.

Never switch model or effort mid chat, you'll bust the cache and the model will have to re-read the whole conversation from scratch. 

I'm on a $20 plan and I have plenty of usage (for my workflow).

comments.author: Vegetable_Voice_2044
comments.body:
Gemini argon will happily burn a third of my daily use in a single prompt if I ask for a large code refactor.
But it also takes a good portion of my own mental energy to read through it all, and make follow up corrections on miscommunications before I just slap the 3-8 modified scripts into my project.

I also have to be very specific about what not to do when I speak to it. If I want a concept review, I have to tell it not to give me code in its reply or it will set my tokens on fire with code I'm not ready for.

Edit: I'm on the $20 subscription

comments.author: aura-32
comments.body:
Workflow is usually the bigger lever. What helped me most: start a fresh chat per task instead of one long conversation, keep a short architecture file the agent reads instead of letting it re-explore the codebase, and ask for plans or reviews in plain text before letting it write code. A loop where two agents review each other's output every step burns tokens fast, so I'd only bring the review agent in when a feature is done.

The same idea ended up shaping our game too. In Hatched (an AI city sim) every citizen runs on a free local rules brain by default, and the model only gets called for moments that matter, like a job offer, a fight or a conversation. Deciding where you actually need the expensive model is most of the battle, in dev and at runtime.

comments.author: fapfap_ahh
comments.body:
Anything that you do repeat, do not have AI keep doing it over and over by itself. Tell it to turn it into a python or shell script that can be used with a skill. Turn that into a memory index that AI can reference.

Common practices, know how, architecture, game play concept, and things if that nature you should keep in a knowledge file (like Claude has Claude.md). Keep it skinny too.

Ask AI to give you feedback on what worked well, what it tripped up on, and ask it to update your knowledge files with that info. You learn as you go with your AI.

Try not to do long running sessions with many big prompts. Split them into smaller tasks and clear the context between or use background agents
